title: Women With PCOS Face Four Times Higher Risk of Heart Disease, Lancet Study Finds
excerpt: A major US study of more than 413,000 women found those with the recently renamed condition had a fourfold increase in cardiovascular disease risk, even after accounting for obesity and diabetes.
body:
• Women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly known as PCOS, face four times the risk of heart disease compared to women without the condition, according to a study published in The Lancet.
  • The US study analysed health insurance data from 413,450 women aged 18 to 50 between 2000 and 2022, matching them against more than two million women without PMOS.
  • The elevated risk persisted even after researchers adjusted for obesity, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes.
  • PCOS prevalence in India ranges from 7% to nearly 20% depending on diagnostic criteria, making the cardiovascular findings especially relevant for South Asian women.

Women diagnosed with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome — the condition formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS — are four times more likely to develop cardiovascular disease than women without the condition, according to a large-scale study published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women's Health.

The research, led by a team at the University of Rochester in New York, analysed US health insurance data spanning more than two decades, from 2000 to 2022. It tracked 413,450 women with the condition, aged between 18 and 50, and matched them against more than two million women who did not have the diagnosis.

The findings were stark: the PMOS group had a fourfold higher risk of heart disease. That elevated risk remained even after the researchers accounted for known cardiovascular risk factors including obesity, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes.

A Condition Renamed, a Problem Reframed

PCOS was officially renamed to PMOS — polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome — in May 2026 following a global push by medical experts who argued the old name placed too much emphasis on ovarian cysts and obscured the condition's broader metabolic and hormonal effects. The renaming aimed to reduce diagnostic delays and shift clinical attention toward the full spectrum of symptoms, which include weight gain, acne, excess hair growth, mood changes, sleep disturbances, and infertility.

Experts had long warned that the narrow framing of the condition as primarily a reproductive issue led to underdiagnosis and inadequate treatment. The UK's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has described the condition as "frequently underdiagnosed and inconsistently managed," estimating it affects between three and four million women in Britain — roughly one in eight.

Cardiovascular Risk Beyond the Usual Suspects

The new study's most significant finding is that the cardiovascular risk associated with PMOS cannot be fully explained by the metabolic comorbidities that often accompany the condition. While women with PMOS frequently have higher rates of insulin resistance, obesity, and type 2 diabetes — all known heart disease risk factors — the fourfold increase in cardiovascular risk persisted independently.

"Our results emphasise the need for physician education and patient awareness of cardiovascular disease risk to improve implementation of early preventive interventions."

— University of Rochester research team, The Lancet

The researchers called for further studies to track women with the condition through menopause, and to explore whether treatments such as GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs or hormonal contraception could modify the link between PMOS and heart disease.

The Lancet study follows a separate large-scale Nordic investigation, led by Professor Dorte Glintborg at the University of Southern Denmark, which tracked 127,517 women with PCOS across Denmark, Finland, and Sweden over an average of 10 years. That study found a 32 percent increase in cardiovascular disease risk — and a 40 percent increase among women of normal weight, suggesting that even those without traditional risk factors are vulnerable.

A Particular Concern for South Asian Women

The findings carry particular weight for women of South Asian descent. A large national survey published in JAMA Network Open found PCOS prevalence in India ranged from 7.2 percent by the strictest diagnostic criteria to nearly 20 percent under the broader Rotterdam criteria. Among those diagnosed, 43 percent were obese, 92 percent had dyslipidemia, and 25 percent had metabolic syndrome — a cluster of conditions that significantly raises heart disease risk.

Studies have also found higher PCOS prevalence in India's metropolitan centres, with rates as high as 22.5 percent in Mumbai and 17.4 percent in Delhi NCR. Researchers have attributed the urban spike partly to the stress, disrupted sleep patterns, and poor dietary habits associated with city life.

For the Indian diaspora, where South Asian women already face elevated baseline cardiovascular risk due to genetic and metabolic factors, the combination with PCOS represents a compounding threat that physicians and patients may be underestimating.

What Comes Next

NICE announced earlier this month that millions of women in the UK with the condition will now be offered annual check-ups to monitor symptoms and manage long-term health risks. The agency recommended that all women with irregular or absent periods and signs of excessive male hormones be investigated for PMOS.

The study authors stressed that preventive measures — including weight management, healthy eating, and regular physical activity — remain critical for reducing cardiovascular risk over time. But they acknowledged that patient surveys consistently report delayed diagnosis and dissatisfaction with the counselling women receive about the condition's long-term consequences.

For the estimated 116 million women worldwide living with the condition, the message from the research is clear: PMOS is not just a reproductive health issue. It is a cardiovascular one.
